lines: Security asks for a role for every team, every dataset, and every environment, calling it least privilege.
Fourteen teams, sixty datasets, three environments. Before I tell you the count, picture what that list actually looks like once someone has to review it.
Here's the shape underneath role-based access control, and it's genuinely this simple.
A role is just a bundle of privileges. A person gets handed one or more of those bundles, instead of being handed privileges one at a time.
That's the whole appeal — manage the bundles, not every individual grant.
So work this one out yourself first.
Fourteen teams, sixty datasets, three environments, and a separate role for every single combination of the three. How many roles does that actually produce?
answer: Over two thousand. Whether or not a team actually touches a given dataset yet, the scheme still hands them a role for it, because it's counting every possible combination, not the realistic handful anyone would use.
That gap between 'every combination' and 'the combinations that matter' is exactly where the number runs away.

lines: And the real number backs that up directly.
Multiply all three out, and you land on two thousand, five hundred and twenty roles. Nobody sits down with a list that size and can honestly say they know who still needs what on it.
Now here's a completely different way to carve up the same problem.

Instead of a role for every combination, write a rule over what things actually are. Analysts can read anything tagged confidential or below. Nobody touches anything tagged personal data without a stated reason for needing it.
One sentence like that does the job of the entire grid.
Try this one before I answer it.

Data science needs a new dataset, and it's got a restricted column. Under the one-role-per-combination scheme, how many new roles does granting that take? And under the one-rule approach, how many edits does the rule itself need?
answer: The role-per-combination scheme needs a fresh role built and assigned for every environment that dataset lives in.
The rule-based approach needs nothing new at all, as long as whoever tagged the new dataset used the same label the rule was already written to read.

lines: And that's borne out directly: one team, three environments, comes out to three brand new roles on one side.
On the other side, zero edits, because the dataset showed up already wearing the tag the rule was watching for.
There's a separation hiding underneath all of this that's easy to miss.
Something has to decide whether a request is allowed. Something else — often a completely different piece of software — has to actually carry that decision out, wherever the data lives.
Keep those two apart, and one decision-maker can answer for every place that needs enforcing, instead of each one reinventing the same logic badly.
None of what we've covered so far knows who anyone actually is.
Something else authenticates a person once, confirming they're really who they claim to be.

A separate piece of machinery creates their accounts across every connected system, and — this is the part that matters — removes them from all of those systems the moment someone pulls the plug in just one place.
One more thing nothing we've built so far catches on its own.
People change teams. Projects wrap up. A rule written for a reason that made sense a year ago keeps quietly granting access long after that reason disappeared.
The only thing that catches that is someone sitting down on a schedule, listing out who has what, and putting their name on each one as still correct.
So here's the whole shape, put back together.

A role for every combination multiplies into thousands, and we measured exactly how fast. One rule over what things actually are replaces the entire grid, and costs nothing new when the next thing already fits the pattern.
Deciding and enforcing stay two separate jobs. And none of it holds up without someone, on a schedule, checking that it still should.
